newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvia central bank strongly backs balanced budget.
newsitem.headline: Latvia central bank strongly backs balanced budget.

text.p: The central bank of the Baltic state of Latvia said on Monday it strongly backed parliament's adoption of a deficit-free 1997 budget.
Latvian central bank chief Einars Repshe urged the adoption of a balanced budget as parliament prepared to start debating the second and final reading of the 1997 budget on Tuesday.
"The Bank of Latvia backs this government project as a turning point in the path of the whole state and for the welfare of each person living in Latvia," Repshe said in a statement.
"Supporting a deficit-free budget at this moment is objectively a necessary decision," Repshe added.
The balanced budget is one of the key objectives of Prime Minister Andris Shkele, a non-party businessman who was brought in as prime minister to sort out the country's finances.
Latvia, which quit the former Soviet Union five years ago, was hit last year by a banking crisis and its deficit rose to 90 million lats -- twice as large as projections.
But the deficit-free budget is controversial as unions say it means ordinary people are making too many sacrifices and spending cuts are being made in areas that need more money.
The planned deficit for 1996 is 40 million lats.
But Repshe said Latvia would gain from balanced budget as it would limit state debt and bring down inflation.
He said that a balanced budget next year could lead to single-digit inflation in 1998. Inflation in November was 0.8 percent month-on-month and 14.4 percent on an annual basis.
"That will allow us to continue to develop business and the economy as a whole, increase the growth of the economy and decrease unemployment," Repshe added.
He said that even a small budget deficit next year could not be allowed as the country was still paying off previous debts and should not borrow more.
He also said that printing money to fund a future deficit was out of the question.
